opus-5.5.text:
I think the two places are complementary rather than redundant. Silicon Valley is still where much of the frontier thinking happens. You're surrounded by researchers, founders, and investors who are trying to figure out what the next platform will be, and that density of ideas is very hard to replicate anywhere else. It's where we stay close to the cutting edge: the newest models, the newest tools, and conversations with people who are setting the direction of the field.

Shenzhen has a different kind of superpower. It's probably the best place in the world to turn an idea into a physical product quickly. The hardware supply chain is right there. You can design something in the morning, get parts from a market down the street in the afternoon, and have a prototype iterated on within days instead of weeks. The engineers there have a very practical, execution-driven mindset. They know manufacturing, cost, and what it takes to ship at scale.

For a company like ours, which sits at the intersection of AI and real-world products, you need both. If you only have the Valley, you may build something brilliant that's hard or expensive to manufacture. If you only have Shenzhen, you may execute very efficiently but on a vision that isn't ambitious enough or isn't aligned with where the technology is heading.

There's also a time-zone benefit that people underestimate. When the US team goes to sleep, the Shenzhen team picks up, so work moves almost around the clock. It isn't without challenges. Communication, culture, and keeping everyone aligned take real effort. You have to be very intentional about building trust across the two teams. But when it works, it's a real advantage: Silicon Valley helps us decide what to build, and Shenzhen helps us build it fast and build it well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Silicon Valley’s frontier ideas and technology, but does not identify tolerance of failure as a cultural strength.

r002.rationale: It says Shenzhen has the hardware supply chain nearby and is exceptionally good at turning ideas into physical products quickly, presenting this as a complementary advantage to Silicon Valley.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Silicon Valley’s frontier focus with Shenzhen’s practical, execution-driven mindset and says a company like theirs needs both, communicating the value of combining those perspectives in its teams.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the two places are good at different things, and the product we're building needs both.

Shenzhen is where hardware actually gets made. If I have an idea for a new board or a mechanical change, I can walk to a supplier in Huaqiangbei, get components the same afternoon, and have a revised prototype in my hands in days instead of weeks. The engineers there have grown up inside that supply chain. They know which factory can hold a tolerance and which one will quietly swap a part. That kind of tacit knowledge is almost impossible to hire for anywhere else. The iteration speed on physical products is just on a different level.

Silicon Valley gives us something different. It's where our early customers and a lot of our investors are, and the software and product talent there has a very strong instinct for what a global user expects, how to design a developer experience, how to think about a platform instead of a one-off device. There's also a culture of thinking big early, which pulls the team toward a larger ambition than we might set for ourselves if we were only optimizing for the next production run.

So the way we split it is roughly: hardware, manufacturing, and supply chain sit in Shenzhen, and product, go-to-market, and a lot of the core software sit in the Valley, with people flying back and forth constantly. The time zone gap is painful, I won't pretend otherwise. But it also means the company is effectively working around the clock, and we've built our processes around clear handoffs rather than live meetings.

The honest risk is cultural drift, where the two offices start to feel like two companies. We fight that by having founders in both places, by rotating engineers between offices for a few months at a time, and by being very explicit about shared goals. When it works, you get the speed of Shenzhen and the reach of Silicon Valley in one company, and I think that combination is genuinely hard for a single-location competitor to match.

r001.rationale: The response describes Silicon Valley’s ambition and product instincts, but does not identify tolerance of failure as a cultural strength.

r002.rationale: It describes Shenzhen’s supplier access, manufacturing knowledge, and faster hardware iteration, contrasting those strengths with Silicon Valley’s distinct strengths.

r003.rationale: The response says this product needs capabilities from both locations, but does not argue that combining people with different ways of thinking is necessary in the current era.

astra-6.text:
For me, the value is that the two places bring different strengths. Shenzhen is a great place to turn an idea into something physical. You can work closely with suppliers, build a prototype, learn what doesn’t work, and iterate quickly. Silicon Valley brings a strong software ecosystem, access to talent and capital, and an environment where people are willing to pursue ambitious ideas.

Having a team in both places lets us connect those strengths. Of course, it creates challenges—time zones, communication, different ways of working. But if we build one team with a shared goal, we can shorten the distance between imagining a product and actually delivering it.

r002.rationale: It mentions working with suppliers in Shenzhen, but does not state that China has a supply-chain advantage over Silicon Valley.

sol-6.1.text:
I see the two places as complementary. Silicon Valley is a great place to understand new technology, talk to customers, and think about what a product could become. Shenzhen gives you access to manufacturing expertise, suppliers, and engineers who can help you turn an idea into something tangible very quickly.

Having a team in each place creates a tighter feedback loop. We can explore a customer need, build a prototype, learn what’s difficult to manufacture, and bring that knowledge back into the design. The time zones and communication take work, but the value is bringing those capabilities together in one team.

r002.rationale: It mentions Shenzhen’s manufacturing expertise and suppliers, but does not identify supply chains as an advantage China has over Silicon Valley.

r003.rationale: It says combining capabilities in one team creates a tighter feedback loop, but does not say people with different ways of thinking are necessary in the current era.
